::: {.callout-note}
## Course Portal: IB Chemistry Higher Level (HL)
Welcome, students! This specialized academic portal provides in-depth resources for the IB Chemistry Higher Level (HL) curriculum. Here, you will find exhaustive syllabus checklists, vertical revision notes, targeted practice question banks, and official subject guides and data booklets—all mathematically and chemically formatted to optimize your learning and help you achieve a Grade 7.
:::

## 1. Course Introduction

<p><strong>IB Chemistry Higher Level (HL)</strong> is a rigorous and highly challenging academic pathway designed for students aiming to pursue careers in Medicine, Pharmacy, Chemical Engineering, or Material Sciences at world-class universities. The curriculum covers the fundamental core concepts (Standard Level Core) along with 95 hours of advanced high-level extension topics (Additional Higher Level - AHL), emphasizing structural models and chemical reactivity.</p>

### Syllabus Structure

<p>The IB Chemistry syllabus is structured around two main pillars: <strong>Structure</strong> (how matter is put together) and <strong>Reactivity</strong> (how matter behaves and reacts). The Higher Level course integrates both the Standard Level core topics and the advanced High-Level extension topics (SL Core & HL Extensions):</p>

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## S1. Models of the particulate nature of matter
**S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter**<br/>
**1.1.1** Elements, compounds, and mixtures.<br/>
**1.1.2** The kinetic molecular theory explains physical properties and state changes.<br/>
**1.1.3** Temperature (K) as a measure of average kinetic energy.<br/>
**S1.2 The nuclear atom**<br/>
**1.2.1** Atomic structure: protons, neutrons, and electrons.<br/>
**1.2.2** Isotopes: same element, different neutron numbers.<br/>
**1.2.3** **[AHL]** Mass spectra determine relative atomic masses.<br/>
**S1.3 Electron configurations**<br/>
**1.3.1** Emission spectra: photons emitted during electron transitions.<br/>
**1.3.2** Hydrogen line spectrum as evidence for discrete energy levels.<br/>
**1.3.3** Main energy level (n) holds a maximum of 2n2 electrons.<br/>
**1.3.4** Main energy level division into s, p, d, and f sublevels.<br/>
**1.3.5** Orbitals hold two electrons of opposite spin; filling principles.<br/>
**1.3.6** **[AHL]** Convergence limit corresponds to ionization.<br/>
**1.3.7** **[AHL]** Successive ionization energy data reveals electron configuration.<br/>
**S1.4 Counting particles by mass: The mole**<br/>
**1.4.1** The mole (mol) and the Avogadro constant.<br/>
**1.4.2** Relative atomic mass (Ar​) and relative formula mass (Mr​).<br/>
**1.4.3** Molar mass (M) in g mol-1.<br/>
**1.4.4** Empirical and molecular formulas.<br/>
**1.4.5** Molar concentration.<br/>
**1.4.6** Avogadro's law for gases.<br/>
**S1.5 Ideal gases**<br/>
**1.5.1** Ideal gas model assumptions.<br/>
**1.5.2** Real gases deviate from the ideal model (low T, high P).<br/>
**1.5.3** Molar volume of an ideal gas.<br/>
**1.5.4** Ideal gas equation (PV=nRT) and combined gas law.<br/>
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## S2. Models of bonding and structure
**S2.1 The ionic model**<br/>
**2.1.1** Cations (from metals) and anions (from non-metals).<br/>
**2.1.2** Ionic bond: electrostatic attraction between ions.<br/>
**2.1.3** Ionic compounds exist as 3D lattice structures.<br/>
**S2.2 The covalent model**<br/>
**2.2.1** Covalent bond: electrostatic attraction for a shared pair of electrons; octet rule.<br/>
**2.2.2** Single, double, and triple bonds (length and strength).<br/>
**2.2.3** Coordination bond: shared pair originates from one atom.<br/>
**2.2.4** VSEPR model predicts molecular shapes.<br/>
**2.2.5** Bond polarity from electronegativity differences.<br/>
**2.2.6** Molecular polarity depends on bond polarity and geometry.<br/>
**2.2.7** Covalent network structures (C allotropes, Si, SiO2​).<br/>
**2.2.8** Intermolecular forces (London, dipole-dipole, H-bonding).<br/>
**2.2.9** Relative strengths of intermolecular forces.<br/>
**2.2.10** Chromatography separates mixtures based on relative attractions.<br/>
**2.2.11** **[AHL]** Resonance structures (delocalization).<br/>
**2.2.12** **[AHL]** Benzene (C6​H6​) structure as an example of resonance.<br/>
**2.2.13** **[AHL]** Atoms with an expanded octet.<br/>
**2.2.14** **[AHL]** Formal charge determines the preferred Lewis formula.<br/>
**2.2.15** **[AHL]** Sigma (σ) bonds (head-on combination) and pi (π) bonds (lateral combination).<br/>
**2.2.16** **[AHL]** Hybridization (sp, sp2, sp3) forms new hybrid orbitals.<br/>
**S2.3 The metallic model**<br/>
**2.3.1** Metallic bond: electrostatic attraction between cations and delocalized electrons.<br/>
**2.3.2** Strength of metallic bond (ion charge, ion radius).<br/>
**2.3.3** **[AHL]** Transition elements have delocalized d-electrons.<br/>
**S2.4 From models to materials**<br/>
**2.4.1** Bonding continuum (ionic, covalent, metallic) represented by a bonding triangle.<br/>
**2.4.2** Position in bonding triangle determined by electronegativity.<br/>
**2.4.3** Alloys: mixtures with enhanced properties.<br/>
**2.4.4** Polymers: macromolecules from repeating monomers.<br/>
**2.4.5** Addition polymers form by breaking double bonds.<br/>
**2.4.6** **[AHL]** Condensation polymers form via reaction between functional groups.<br/>
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## S3. Classification of matter
**S3.1 The periodic table: Classification of elements**<br/>
**3.1.1** Periodic table structure: periods, groups, blocks.<br/>
**3.1.2** Period number (outer energy level) and group number (valence electrons).<br/>
**3.1.3** Periodicity: trends in properties (radius, IE, electronegativity).<br/>
**3.1.4** Trends in Group 1 (alkali metals) and Group 17 (halogens).<br/>
**3.1.5** Continuum of properties (metallic/non-metallic); oxide trends.<br/>
**3.1.6** Oxidation state: assigned number (charge if ionic).<br/>
**3.1.7** **[AHL]** Discontinuities in first IE as evidence for sublevels.<br/>
**3.1.8** **[AHL]** Transition element properties from incomplete d-sublevels.<br/>
**3.1.9** **[AHL]** Variable oxidation states in transition elements.<br/>
**3.1.10** **[AHL]** Coloured complexes due to d-sublevel splitting.<br/>
**S3.2 Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds**<br/>
**3.2.1** Representation of organic compounds (formulas, models).<br/>
**3.2.2** Functional groups give characteristic properties.<br/>
**3.2.3** Homologous series: family differing by a structural unit (e.g., CH2​).<br/>
**3.2.4** Trends in physical properties within a homologous series.<br/>
**3.2.5** IUPAC nomenclature (systematic names).<br/>
**3.2.6** Structural isomers (same formula, different connectivity).<br/>
**3.2.7** **[AHL]** Stereoisomers (cis-trans and optical isomers/enantiomers).<br/>
**3.2.8** **[AHL]** Mass spectrometry (MS) fragmentation patterns.<br/>
**3.2.9** **[AHL]** Infrared (IR) spectra identify bond types.<br/>
**3.2.10** **[AHL]** Proton nuclear magnetic resonance (¹H NMR) shows H environments.<br/>
**3.2.11** **[AHL]** ¹H NMR splitting patterns (singlets, doublets, etc.).<br/>
**3.2.12** **[AHL]** Combined data for structural determination.<br/>
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## R1. What drives chemical reactions?
**R1.1 Measuring enthalpy changes**<br/>
**1.1.1** Chemical reactions involve energy transfer; total energy conserved.<br/>
**1.1.2** Endothermic (energy absorbed) and exothermic (energy released) reactions.<br/>
**1.1.3** Relative stability of reactants/products determines endo/exothermic.<br/>
**1.1.4** Standard enthalpy change (ΔH⊖) determined from temperature change (Q=mcΔT).<br/>
**R1.2 Energy cycles in reactions**<br/>
**1.2.1** Bond-breaking absorbs energy; bond-forming releases energy (average bond enthalpy).<br/>
**1.2.2** Hess's law: enthalpy change is pathway independent.<br/>
**1.2.3** **[AHL]** Standard enthalpy changes of combustion (ΔHc⊖​) and formation (ΔHf⊖​).<br/>
**1.2.4** **[AHL]** Calculating ΔH⊖ using ΔHf⊖​ or ΔHc⊖​ data.<br/>
**1.2.5** **[AHL]** Born-Haber cycle (application of Hess's law for ionic compounds).<br/>
**R1.3 Energy from fuels**<br/>
**1.3.1** Combustion reactions occur when heated in oxygen.<br/>
**1.3.2** Incomplete combustion produces CO and/or C.<br/>
**1.3.3** Fossil fuels (advantages and disadvantages).<br/>
**1.3.4** Biofuels (from biological fixation of carbon).<br/>
**1.3.5** Fuel cells convert chemical energy to electrical energy.<br/>
**R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (AHL)**<br/>
**1.4.1** **[AHL]** Entropy (S): measure of matter/energy dispersal.<br/>
**1.4.2** **[AHL]** Gibbs energy: ΔG⊖=ΔH⊖−TΔS⊖.<br/>
**1.4.3** **[AHL]** Spontaneous change occurs if ΔG is negative.<br/>
**1.4.4** **[AHL]** At equilibrium, ΔG=0; ΔG⊖=−RTlnK.<br/>
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## R2. How much, how fast and how far?
**R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change**<br/>
**2.1.1** Chemical equations show reactant/product ratios.<br/>
**2.1.2** Mole ratios determine masses, volumes, or concentrations.<br/>
**2.1.3** Limiting reactant determines theoretical yield.<br/>
**2.1.4** Percentage yield (experimental/theoretical).<br/>
**2.1.5** Atom economy (measure of efficiency).<br/>
**R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change**<br/>
**2.2.1** Rate of reaction: change in concentration per unit time.<br/>
**2.2.2** Collision theory: requires sufficient energy and proper orientation.<br/>
**2.2.3** Factors influencing reaction rate (pressure, conc, surface area, temp, catalyst).<br/>
**2.2.4** Activation energy (Ea​): minimum energy for successful collision.<br/>
**2.2.5** Catalysts provide an alternative pathway with lower Ea​.<br/>
**2.2.6** **[AHL]** Reaction mechanisms occur in elementary steps; slowest step is rate-determining.<br/>
**2.2.7** **[AHL]** Energy profiles for multistep reactions.<br/>
**2.2.8** **[AHL]** Molecularity (unimolecular, bimolecular, termolecular).<br/>
**2.2.9** **[AHL]** Rate equations determined experimentally.<br/>
**2.2.10** **[AHL]** Order of reaction (zero, first, second).<br/>
**2.2.11** **[AHL]** Rate constant (k) is temperature dependent.<br/>
**2.2.12** **[AHL]** Arrhenius equation relates k, T, and Ea​.<br/>
**2.2.13** **[AHL]** Arrhenius factor (A).<br/>
**R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change**<br/>
**2.3.1** Dynamic equilibrium: closed system, forward/backward rates equal.<br/>
**2.3.2** Equilibrium law and equilibrium constant (K).<br/>
**2.3.3** Magnitude of K indicates reaction extent; temperature dependent.<br/>
**2.3.4** Le Châtelier's principle predicts effects of changes.<br/>
**2.3.5** **[AHL]** Reaction quotient (Q) predicts direction of shift.<br/>
**2.3.6** **[AHL]** Solving equilibrium problems (calculating concentrations).<br/>
**2.3.7** **[AHL]** Relationship between K and ΔG.<br/>
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## R3. What are the mechanisms of chemical change?
**R3.1 Proton transfer reactions**<br/>
**3.1.1** Brønsted-Lowry acid (proton donor) and base (proton acceptor).<br/>
**3.1.2** Conjugate acid-base pair (differ by one proton).<br/>
**3.1.3** Amphiprotic species (act as acid or base).<br/>
**3.1.4** The pH scale: pH=−log10​[H+].<br/>
**3.1.5** Ion product constant of water (Kw​=[H+][OH−]).<br/>
**3.1.6** Strong vs. weak acids/bases (extent of ionization).<br/>
**3.1.7** Neutralization reactions (acid + base).<br/>
**3.1.8** pH curves for strong acid-strong base titrations.<br/>
**3.1.9** **[AHL]** The pOH scale: pOH=−log10​[OH−].<br/>
**3.1.10** **[AHL]** Ka​,Kb​,pKa​,pKb​ describe weak acid/base strength.<br/>
**3.1.11** **[AHL]** Relationship for conjugate pairs: Ka​×Kb​=Kw​.<br/>
**3.1.12** **[AHL]** pH of salt solutions (hydrolysis).<br/>
**3.1.13** **[AHL]** pH curves for all strong/weak combinations.<br/>
**3.1.14** **[AHL]** Acid-base indicators are weak acids.<br/>
**3.1.15** **[AHL]** Choosing an appropriate indicator (end point vs. equivalence point).<br/>
**3.1.16** **[AHL]** Buffer solutions resist pH change.<br/>
**3.1.17** **[AHL]** pH of a buffer solution (depends on pKa​/pKb​ and concentration ratio).<br/>
**R3.2 Electron transfer reactions**<br/>
**3.2.1** Oxidation and reduction definitions (e- transfer, oxidation state).<br/>
**3.2.2** Half-equations show oxidation and reduction separately.<br/>
**3.2.3** Predicting redox ease from periodic table position.<br/>
**3.2.4** Acids react with reactive metals to release H2​.<br/>
**3.2.5** Anode (oxidation) and cathode (reduction) in electrochemical cells.<br/>
**3.2.6** Primary (voltaic) cells (spontaneous redox).<br/>
**3.2.7** Secondary (rechargeable) cells (reversible redox).<br/>
**3.2.8** Electrolytic cells (non-spontaneous redox).<br/>
**3.2.9** Oxidation of organic compounds (alcohols).<br/>
**3.2.10** Reduction of organic compounds (carboxylic acids, ketones).<br/>
**3.2.11** Reduction of unsaturated compounds (addition of H2​).<br/>
**3.2.12** **[AHL]** Standard electrode potential (E⊖) (relative to H2​ half-cell).<br/>
**3.2.13** **[AHL]** Standard cell potential (E⊖cell​); positive for spontaneous reactions.<br/>
**3.2.14** **[AHL]** Relationship: ΔG⊖=−nFE⊖.<br/>
**3.2.15** **[AHL]** Electrolysis of aqueous solutions (competing reactions).<br/>
**3.2.16** **[AHL]** Electroplating.<br/>
**R3.3 Electron sharing reactions**<br/>
**3.3.1** Radicals: molecular entities with an unpaired electron.<br/>
**3.3.2** Radicals produced by homolytic fission (UV or heat).<br/>
**3.3.3** Radicals take part in substitution reactions with alkanes.<br/>
**R3.4 Electron-pair sharing reactions**<br/>
**3.4.1** Nucleophile: reactant that donates an electron pair.<br/>
**3.4.2** Nucleophilic substitution: nucleophile donates e- pair, leaving group departs.<br/>
**3.4.3** Heterolytic fission: bond breaks, both electrons go to one fragment.<br/>
**3.4.4** Electrophile: reactant that accepts an electron pair.<br/>
**3.4.5** Electrophilic addition: alkenes susceptible due to high e- density.<br/>
**3.4.6** **[AHL]** Lewis acid (e- pair acceptor) and Lewis base (e- pair donor).<br/>
**3.4.7** **[AHL]** Lewis acid-base reactions form coordination bonds.<br/>
**3.4.8** **[AHL]** Ligands (Lewis bases) form complex ions with transition elements.<br/>
**3.4.9** **[AHL]** Nucleophilic substitution mechanisms (SN​1, SN​2).<br/>
**3.4.10** **[AHL]** Rate of substitution influenced by the leaving group.<br/>
**3.4.11** **[AHL]** Electrophilic addition mechanisms (symmetrical alkenes).<br/>
**3.4.12** **[AHL]** Carbocation stability (unsymmetrical alkenes); major product.<br/>
**3.4.13** **[AHL]** Electrophilic substitution mechanisms (benzene).<br/>
:::
